> **What this case shows** — coherence (the sibling case) tells you two signals are
> coupled, but not which *leads*. **Granger causality** adds the arrow: a signal
> *x* Granger-causes *y* if *x*'s past improves the prediction of *y* beyond *y*'s own
> past. On a real simultaneous **respiration + PPG** recording, the ecosystem's
> `grangerCausality` measures the coupling in **both directions at once** and finds it
> strong and **bidirectional** — cardiorespiratory coupling runs both ways — with
> **respiration → pulse** the net-dominant direction (respiration modulating the
> peripheral pulse) in **15 of 20** BIDMC subjects. And the measure is trustworthy:
> `grangerCausality` reproduces the field-standard `statsmodels` Granger test to
> **~3.5e-7** (an agreement, limited by an intercept convention) and an independent
> from-scratch OLS to **~1.8e-9**, both directions — and `statsmodels`' F-test confirms
> both directions are overwhelmingly significant (F ≈ 54, p < 1e-100).

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — for directed coupling between two signals:
`grangerCausality(x, y, order)` → read `gc_xy` (x→y), `gc_yx` (y→x), and `net_gc` (the
asymmetry) in one call.
**Way of thinking** — Granger causality is *predictive* coupling: does the past of one
signal help forecast another? It is temporal precedence, **not** proof of a physical
cause. Read the *net* direction, and remember coupling is usually two-way.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioCrossModal::grangerCausality()`, with a `method =
"nonparametric"` spectral path (`partialDirectedCoherence()` / `directedTransferFunction()`
for the frequency-resolved, multivariate cases).
:::

## Proposition

On real simultaneous respiration + PPG (BIDMC), time-domain Granger causality is strong
and bidirectional, with respiration → pulse net-dominant in 15/20 subjects, and
`grangerCausality` reproduces `statsmodels.tsa.stattools.grangercausalitytests` (~3.5e-7)
and an independent numpy OLS (~1.8e-9) on the real signals, both directions.

## Question & goal

**The question is directional: does respiration drive the peripheral pulse, the pulse
drive respiration, or both — and does the ecosystem measure it the way the field-standard
tool does?** Coherence cannot answer the first part (it is symmetric). Granger causality
can. The goal is a head-to-head of `grangerCausality` against `statsmodels`, and a clear
read of the arrow on real cardiorespiratory data.

## Challenge & approach

Time-domain Granger causality fits two OLS regressions per direction — the target on its
own lagged past (restricted), and on its past *plus* the driver's past (unrestricted) —
and takes **GC = log(var_restricted / var_unrestricted)** (Geweke's measure). We compute
both directions with `grangerCausality`, and re-compute each with `statsmodels`
(restricted/unrestricted SSRs) and an independent from-scratch numpy OLS.

```
RESP, PLETH (BIDMC, 25 Hz) → grangerCausality(order=10) → gc_xy, gc_yx, net_gc
                                                          vs statsmodels grangercausalitytests
                                                          vs independent numpy OLS
                                                          → agreement + F-test + net direction
```

## Data

**BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset (PhysioNet)**: subject **bidmc01**, simultaneous
**RESP** (impedance-pneumography respiration) and **PLETH** (fingertip PPG), decimated
125→25 Hz, a 200 s segment (5001 samples). The net-direction summary repeats the same
extraction on **bidmc01–bidmc20**. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: on BIDMC-01, the two directional Granger magnitudes (respiration→pulse and pulse→respiration) computed three ways — grangerCausality (blue), statsmodels (orange), and an independent numpy OLS (grey) — sit on top of each other (max |op − statsmodels| = 3.5e-7, max |op − numpy OLS| = 1.8e-9). Right: the net Granger causality (respiration→pulse minus pulse→respiration) across 20 BIDMC subjects, sorted; 15 of 20 are positive (green) — respiration → pulse is the net-dominant direction — while 5 (red) run the other way, so the coupling is genuinely bidirectional.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* the left panel is the **validation** — three independent
implementations agree. The right panel is the **finding** — a mostly-positive net
Granger causality: respiration tends to drive the peripheral pulse, but not exclusively.

| Quantity | This reproduction | Reference |
|---|---|---|
| GC respiration → pulse (BIDMC-01) | **0.1031** | statsmodels 0.1031 |
| GC pulse → respiration (BIDMC-01) | **0.1017** | statsmodels 0.1017 |
| net GC (respiration → pulse) | **+0.0015** | — |
| max \|op − statsmodels\| (both directions) | **3.5e-7** | 0 (agreement) |
| max \|op − independent numpy OLS\| | **1.8e-9** | 0 (op's ridge floor) |
| statsmodels F (both directions) | **54.0 / 53.2**, p < 1e-100 | both significant |
| respiration → pulse net-dominant | **15 / 20 subjects** | — |

Both directions are strong and significant; the net arrow points respiration → pulse in
the majority. Values trace to
[`artifacts/granger_summary.csv`](artifacts/granger_summary.csv) and the per-subject table
in [`artifacts/granger_multisubject.csv`](artifacts/granger_multisubject.csv).

## Conclusion

The ecosystem's Granger causality is the same measure `statsmodels` computes — to a
convention-limited 3.5e-7, and to 1.8e-9 against an independent OLS — and it reads the
arrow on real cardiorespiratory data: coupling is bidirectional, with respiration → pulse
net-dominant in most subjects. The transferable takeaway: **use Granger causality when you
need direction, not just coupling; read the *net* magnitude and treat it as predictive
precedence, not physical cause; and validate the estimator against the field-standard tool
before trusting the arrow.**

## Open questions

- `grangerCausality` also implements a **nonparametric spectral** path (Wilson
  minimum-phase factorization of the cross-spectrum), giving **frequency-resolved** Granger
  causality — which would show *where* in the spectrum (the respiratory band vs the cardiac
  band) each direction dominates, and a **conditional/multivariate** GC would separate
  direct from mediated coupling. Extending this to the spectral and conditional cases — and
  to a respiration → instantaneous-heart-rate (RSA) tachogram design where the direction is
  textbook — would turn a validated pairwise op into a network-physiology study.
  *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| directed coupling, two signals (time domain) | `grangerCausality()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| frequency-resolved directed coupling | `grangerCausality(method = "nonparametric")` | PhysioCrossModal |
| multivariate directed connectivity | `partialDirectedCoherence()` / `directedTransferFunction()` | PhysioCrossModal |
| symmetric coupling (the sibling measure) | `coherence()` | PhysioCrossModal |

**Choosing the parameters.**

- **order** — the number of lags in the autoregressive models (here 10, ≈ 400 ms at
  25 Hz); it sets how far back the "past" reaches. Too small misses slow coupling; too
  large overfits. Match it to the timescale of the coupling you expect.
- **sr** — the sampling rate; it does not change the time-domain GC value, but it sets the
  physical meaning of `order` (lags × 1/sr seconds).
- **direction** — `grangerCausality` returns *both* directions and their difference in one
  call; read `net_gc` for the asymmetry, and never read a single direction as "the cause".

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioCrossModal)

g <- grangerCausality(resp, pleth, sr = 25, order = 10)
g$gc_xy      # respiration -> pulse   (0.1031)
g$gc_yx      # pulse -> respiration   (0.1017)
g$net_gc     # net direction          (+0.0015: respiration -> pulse dominates)

# reproduces statsmodels.tsa.stattools.grangercausalitytests (~3.5e-7) and an
# independent OLS (~1.8e-9), both directions.
```
